extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, and researchers of British comedy/satire (readers of Wikipedia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the stylistic and production qualities exemplified by Chris Morris's work (radio, television, film) that define effective satirical comedy—delivery, formats, techniques, risks and aims. Useful for understanding how edgy, surreal, spoof-news satire is constructed and received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan delivery
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadpan delivery lends credibility and normalcy to absurd or shocking material; used across radio and television projects (e.g., On the Hour, The Day Today) to heighten satirical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of dark humour that treats upsetting or taboo subjects comically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dark humour allows satire to address serious social issues (e.g., paedophilia, terrorism) but carries risk of strong public backlash and complaints (the 'Paedogeddon' Brass Eye episode received ~3,000 complaints and an apology from Channel 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrealism and postmodern sketch approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism and postmodern sketch comedy are central elements of his style (e.g., Blue Jam, Jam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surreal or postmodern structures (non-linear, unsettling, ambient soundscapes) create a distinct tone and cult following; they can be adapted between radio and television to maintain mood (Blue Jam → Jam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial/taboo subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate engagement with controversial and taboo topics as subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tackling taboo topics can reveal cultural hypocrisies or moral panics but may provoke media condemnation and viewer complaints; practitioners should weigh satirical purpose against likely consequences (public complaints, tabloid reactions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoof news format
rubrics_metrics.description: Development and use of the spoof news format to lampoon news programmes and current-affairs rhetoric (On the Hour, The Day Today, Brass Eye).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerate news conventions and political rhetoric to expose absurdities. The spoof-news frame provides authority that can be subverted to satirise institutions, public figures, and media-driven moral panics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prank/unsuspecting-public interviews and ‘spoof interview’ technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Odd interviews conducted with unsuspecting members of the public and spoof interview styles perfected across radio shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using unsuspecting interviewees heightens realism and exposes genuine reactions, but can cause professional consequences (e.g., suspension/firing) and ethical concerns; approvals and editorial safeguards may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo-breaking and shock tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of crass, shocking material and taboo-breaking for comedic and satirical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shock can be an instrument to underline satire's point; critics note that Morris pairs shock with an 'underlying morality' or purpose. However, shock without clear satirical aim risks being perceived as gratuitous and provoking public outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying moralistic/intellectual drive
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'uncompromising, moralistic drive' or underlying morality often underpins the provocative material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective provocative satire typically has a recognisable critique or moral aim rather than mere provocation; reviewers credit Morris's work for having integrity and purpose beneath crassness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ambient music and sound design
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration of ambient soundtracks and music to set tone (notably Blue Jam / Jam and incidental music contributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound design and music reinforce surreal atmosphere and emotional texture; they can transform radio pieces into distinctive audio experiences and support transitions to television or film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive deceptive devices (fabricated elements to test/ expose reactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of fabricated elements (e.g., fictional drug 'cake') to satirise policy, rhetoric, or public gullibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invented constructs can reveal how politicians, media, and public respond to claims; such devices are effective to demonstrate absurdity but may implicate those tricked and invite controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushing boundaries to discover truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy: 'If you make a joke in an area which is ... out of bounds, then you might find something out, you might put your finger on something.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional boundary-pushing is presented as a method to surface hidden assumptions or hypocrisies; practitioners should balance risk and insight, and be prepared for strong reactions when probing sensitive topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation across media (radio → television → film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques and formats adapted between radio, television and film (e.g., Blue Jam adapted into Jam; radio spoof-news spawning TV spinoffs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful satirical devices can be translated across media but require tailoring (visuals, pacing, production values). Adaptation can broaden reach and impact but also changes audience expectations and potential for controversy.
